openingProblem.problem: In 1975 Spain had been ruled by one dictator for thirty-six years. By 1982 the party of his former opponents governed after free elections. How did a dictatorship become a democracy without a revolution?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: who made Spanish democracy?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Franco's Spain: Church, army and control, 1939–1975
chunks.body:
General Franco came to power by a military coup in 1936 and, after victory in the Civil War, ruled Spain unchallenged from 1939 until his death in 1975. His regime rested on three supports: the Catholic Church, the army and the police.

The Church gave the regime its ideas. In a **concordat of 1953** Franco granted the Church exemption from taxation and from all state interference, and even a right to demand the censorship of any writing or speech it disliked. In return the bishops taught that to be Catholic was to be Spanish. The leading primary-school history book, *Yo soy español* ('I am Spanish', first published in 1943), told the nation's story as a single line from the Garden of Eden to the Generalissimo. Tony Judt argues that Franco needed the Church even more than it needed him, because Catholicism was his link to the West.

The army was flattered rather than used. Its Civil War victory was celebrated every year, and its dead were honoured in the vast Valley of the Fallen, completed in 1959. By the end of the regime there were 300 generals and one officer for every eleven men, the highest ratio in Europe; a law of 1967 made the armed forces responsible for defending "the institutional system". Yet Franco kept the army out of wars, and it became largely ceremonial. Its conservatism showed itself in enthusiasm for the return of the monarchy.

Control was tight. Independent political parties were banned, and until 1967 Spain had no constitution at all. Censorship was rigid, the police were everywhere and the penal laws for political critics were draconian. As late as 1963 Franco had a captured Communist, Juan Grimau, executed despite international protests. Everything distinctively Basque (language, customs, politics) was repressed, and by the early 1970s a quarter of Spain's armed police were stationed in the Basque country. In December 1958 Basque radicals formed ETA to fight for independence, a direct response, Judt says, to Franco's policies.

By its last years, however, the regime relied less on open violence than on what Judt calls "enforced passive acceptance", a long de-politicisation of public life. Officially Franco was a "regent" for a suspended monarchy, and he chose the young Juan Carlos, grandson of Spain's last king, to succeed him. This mattered because Francoism had no political life of its own beyond Franco, which meant that when he died its institutions could be dismantled by the very men he had appointed.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Church gave the regime legitimacy and its link to the West.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: By the late 1960s religion itself was in decline and the hierarchy was kept away from power.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The army was cosseted but kept out of politics and wars.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Its legal duty to defend 'the institutional system' made it a potential threat to change.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Repression was real, especially against Basques and Communists.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: In the last years the regime relied more on passive acceptance than open violence.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Franco maintained his rule above all by binding the Church and the army to the regime.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The concordat of 1953 freed the Church from taxation and gave it a right to demand censorship, while the army was flattered with 300 generals and a legal duty to defend 'the institutional system'.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the two most powerful institutions in Spain had a stake in the regime, so neither became a centre of opposition.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, repression also mattered: parties were banned, Grimau was executed in 1963 and Basque culture was suppressed.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Franco's rule therefore rested on institutional loyalty first and repression second, which is why, by its last years, passive acceptance was enough.

chunks.title: The economic opening and social change, 1959–1975
chunks.body:
Franco was a rigid, reactionary dictator, Judt writes, but also an economic realist. For two decades Spain had tried to live by **autarky**, protected from foreign competition. In 1959, at the urging of a group of ministers from the Catholic organisation Opus Dei, the regime changed course and adopted a **National Stabilization Plan** to curb inflation and open Spain to trade and investment. The first effects were harsh: devaluation, budget cuts, a credit freeze and wage restrictions. Tens of thousands of Spaniards had to look for work abroad.

Then growth came. Tariffs were cut and Spain joined the World Bank, the IMF and GATT; in 1962 Franco even applied, without success, to join the EEC. From 1961 national output rose steadily. In 1950 one Spanish worker in two had worked on the land; by 1971 it was one in five, as labourers from the south and west moved north into factories and the booming tourist trade. Tourism exploded: French visitors rose from a few thousand in 1955 to seven million in 1964, and the total number of foreign visitors rose from 17.3 million in 1966 to 34 million in the year before Franco's death. By the mid-1960s Spain no longer counted as a "developing nation" under UN criteria.

Judt warns against overstating this "economic miracle". Most foreign money came not from Spanish exports but from emigrants' remittances and holiday-makers, so modernisation was "largely a by-product of other nations' prosperity". In 1973 income per head was still below Ireland's and less than half the EEC average.

But the social effects were large. From the later 1960s strikes, lockouts and demonstrations became a fixture of Spanish life. With millions of foreigners watching, the regime could not afford to look too repressive, and it needed the skills of the new urban workforce, so it had to tolerate an unofficial labour movement in Catalonia and the Basque heavy industries. By 1975 this network had nearly a decade of experience. Religion declined too. In June 1968 Franco conceded the principle of religious freedom; the number of seminarists fell from over 8,000 at the start of the 1960s to under 2,000 twelve years later.

This mattered because, as Judt argues, by 1975 it was the political state, not Spanish society, that had fallen behind, which meant that democracy, when it came, fitted a society that had already changed.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It still transformed the structure of the workforce.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Economic change created a labour movement and weakened the Church's hold.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Labour protest was confined to bread-and-butter issues, not politics.

chunks.title: The transition from above, 1975–1978
chunks.body:
Even before Franco died, Americans were asking what would follow. In May 1975 a secret US intelligence memorandum, "Spain: Problems of the Succession", put the dilemma in one sentence: "the regime must change in order to survive but any real change carries threats to its existence." It judged a radical upheaval unlikely, but its forecast depended heavily on the army's role as a deterrent.

Franco died on 20 November 1975, aged 82. Two days later **Juan Carlos** was crowned king. At first he kept Franco's last Prime Minister, Carlos Arias Navarro, to reassure the army that there would be no sudden break. But in April 1976 Arias arrested the leaders of the Democratic Coordination, a coalition of still-illegal left-wing parties, and within two months the king replaced him with **Adolfo Suárez**. Judt stresses that the transition was managed "from within the ranks of Franco's own ministers and appointees", which helps explain its speed and success; the opposition at first played a subordinate role.

Suárez seemed an unlikely reformer. Aged 44, he was a late-Franco technocrat who had headed the regime's own National Movement for a year. He formed a new party, the Centre Democratic Union (UCD), and persuaded the Francoist assembly to accept a referendum on political reform, introducing universal suffrage and a two-chamber parliament. Wrong-footed by a man they took for one of their own, the old guard agreed, and on 15 December 1976 the reform passed with over 94 per cent of the vote. In 1977 the pace quickened. In February the Socialist Party (PSOE), led by the young Felipe González, was allowed back and trade unions won the right to strike. On 1 April Suárez dismantled the National Movement; a week later he legalised the Communist Party of Santiago Carrillo.

In June 1977 Spain held its first elections since 1936. The UCD won 165 seats, the Socialists 121 and all others 67. Judt calls this the best possible outcome: conservatives were reassured, while Suárez, without a majority, had to share responsibility for the new constitution with the left. The **Constitution**, approved by referendum in December 1978, made Spain a parliamentary monarchy with no official religion, lowered the voting age to eighteen, abolished the death penalty and gave the historic regions, above all Catalonia and the Basque country, a right to autonomy.

Judt's judgement is ironic: democracy was made possible "not by cultural or political radicals" but by conservative men of the old regime, whose reassurance to their own side allowed them to dismantle the institutions they had served. This mattered because a transition from above avoided a violent break, which meant that Spain changed its system without reopening the Civil War.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The opposition's pressure and strikes also pushed the pace.

chunks.title: Threats and consolidation, 1977–1982
chunks.body:
The new democracy faced three dangers: the economy, terrorism and the army.

The economy was in crisis. The last Franco governments had bought popularity with public spending and subsidies, and by June 1977 inflation was running at 26 per cent a year. Spain lost an estimated 1.8 million jobs between 1973 and 1982. The **Moncloa Pacts** of October 1977, agreed by politicians, labour leaders and employers, brought devaluation, an incomes policy and controls on spending. Judt says they "worked no miracles", but without them the divisions would almost certainly have been worse.

Terrorism grew. ETA had already assassinated Franco's Prime Minister, Admiral Carrero Blanco, in Madrid in December 1973. It wanted full independence, and when the Basque country was given a Statute of Autonomy, approved by referendum in 1979, it stepped up its campaign: in 1979–80 it killed 181 people. It aimed to provoke a backlash that would bring down democracy.

In 1981 it nearly did. On 29 January Suárez was forced out by his own party, and a general strike broke out in the Basque provinces. To the right, Spain looked leaderless and close to breaking up. On **23 February 1981** Lieutenant Colonel Antonio Tejero of the Civil Guard seized the Cortes at gunpoint, while General Jaime Milans del Bosch declared a state of emergency in Valencia and called on the king to dissolve parliament and install a military government. Judt notes that the parties could have done little to stop a military coup, and the army's sympathies were uncertain.

What decided the outcome was **King Juan Carlos**. He rejected the conspirators' demands and, in a televised speech, defended the Constitution and identified the monarchy with the democratic majority. With no institution to rally around, most of those nostalgic for the old regime turned instead to Manuel Fraga's Popular Alliance, within the law. Afterwards the Cortes cut the military budget and legalised divorce.

Democracy then passed its final test. In October 1982 the Socialists won an absolute majority and Felipe González became Prime Minister. Suárez's UCD, which had led the transition, won just two seats. Power had passed peacefully to the party of the former opposition. This mattered because alternation in power showed that democracy no longer depended on the men of the old regime, which meant that Spanish politics now looked like the rest of western Europe.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Unemployment and inflation still rose, provoking strikes.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Its violence helped create the mood in which the coup was attempted.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The king's stand in 1981 and the peaceful change of government in 1982 consolidated democracy.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The coup showed how fragile democracy still was.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was the economic opening of 1959 responsible for the transition to democracy in Spain between 1959 and 1978?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: How far the economy, rather than political choices, caused democracy

modelPlan.thesis: The economic opening was a necessary condition of democracy, because it created a modern, urban society with its own labour movement; but political choices after 1975 decided the form and speed of the transition.

arguments.claim: Economic opening transformed society (named factor first).
A labour movement and the decline of the Church.
Political choices: the king and Suárez.

modelPlan.counter: The transition was managed from within the regime, so political leadership, not the economy, explains how it happened.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Could democracy have taken root without the changes of 1959–1975? Judt suggests not, because society had already moved ahead of the state.

segments.text: The economic opening of 1959 made democracy possible by changing Spanish society faster than the Spanish state.
The share of workers on the land fell from one in two in 1950 to one in five in 1971, and by 1975 an unofficial labour movement had nearly a decade of experience.
This meant that the regime faced a modern society it could not simply repress, so its survival without Franco became unlikely.
However, the transition itself was managed by Franco's own appointees, and the king's choice of Suárez decided its course.
The economic opening was therefore necessary but not sufficient: it explains why democracy came, while political choices explain how.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “The transition to democracy in Spain was made from above.” Discuss with reference to the period 1975 to 1978.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: How far the old regime's men, rather than the opposition, made democracy

modelPlan.thesis: The transition was begun from above, by the king and Suárez using Francoist institutions, but it was completed by negotiation with a legalised opposition that helped write the Constitution.

arguments.claim: For: the king appointed an insider.
For: Francoist institutions voted for reform.
Against: the opposition shaped the elections and Constitution.
Against: consensus with the left in the Constitution.

modelPlan.counter: Strikes from the later 1960s, and demonstrations in 1975 demanding freedom of the press and of political association, show pressure from below.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Who decided the content of democracy? The Constitution was negotiated with the left, so 'from above' describes the start more than the finish.

segments.text: The transition was begun from above, by men the dictatorship had itself appointed.
Juan Carlos appointed Suárez, a former head of the National Movement, who persuaded the Francoist assembly to accept a reform referendum that passed with over 94 per cent on 15 December 1976.
This meant that the old regime's institutions voted for their own reform, so its supporters were reassured and the army had no grounds to act.
However, once legalised, the Socialists won 121 seats in 1977 and shared in writing the Constitution, so the opposition shaped the final settlement.
The claim is therefore valid for how the transition began, but not for how it ended.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the success of the transition to democracy in Spain between 1975 and 1982.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: By what criterion: institutions, survival, or alternation in power

modelPlan.thesis: The transition largely succeeded: it built a consensual constitution and ended in a peaceful change of government in 1982, though ETA's violence and the 1981 coup attempt showed how fragile it remained.
modelPlan.counter: The coup attempt of 1981 showed that democracy survived only because of one man's decision.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: By the test of alternation in power, the transition succeeded, because the former opposition took office peacefully in 1982.

segments.text: The transition largely succeeded, because by 1982 power had passed peacefully to the former opposition.
The 1978 Constitution was approved by referendum, the coup of February 1981 failed, and in October 1982 the Socialists won an absolute majority.
This meant that democracy no longer depended on the men of the old regime, so it had become a normal western European system.
However, ETA killed 181 people in 1979–80 and inflation reached 26 per cent in 1977, so the new democracy was fragile.
The transition was therefore a success by the decisive test of alternation, despite the dangers it survived.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the methods Franco used to maintain his rule in Spain between 1939 and 1975.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which method mattered most, and how the methods changed over time

modelPlan.thesis: Franco ruled above all by binding the Church and the army to the regime, backed by repression; in his last years enforced passive acceptance and economic growth replaced open violence.
modelPlan.counter: Economic growth after 1959 created the social forces that the regime could no longer fully control.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which method lasted? Institutional loyalty, since repression gave way to passive acceptance in the last years.

segments.text: Franco maintained his rule above all by binding the Church and the army to the regime.
The 1953 concordat freed the Church from taxation and gave it a right to request censorship, while the army had 300 generals and a legal duty to defend 'the institutional system'.
This meant that Spain's most powerful institutions had a stake in the regime, so neither became a centre of opposition.
However, repression also mattered: parties were banned, Grimau was executed in 1963 and Basque culture was suppressed.
Institutional loyalty was therefore Franco's main method, with repression its support and, later, passive acceptance its result.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the causes and consequences of political instability in Spain between 1979 and 1982.

decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: Instability was caused mainly by ETA's terror and the economic crisis, which left the government looking leaderless; its most significant consequence was paradoxical: the failed coup of 1981 strengthened democracy.

arguments.claim: Cause: the economic crisis and Suárez's fall.
Consequence: the coup attempt and the king's stand.

modelPlan.counter: The coup showed how close democracy came to failure, since the parties could have done little to stop it.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted? The king's identification with the Constitution, which removed the old right's rallying point.

segments.text: Instability was caused above all by ETA's terror, which aimed to provoke a backlash.
ETA killed 181 people in 1979–80, while Spain lost 1.8 million jobs between 1973 and 1982 and Suárez was forced out in January 1981.
This meant that to the right democratic Spain looked leaderless and close to breaking up, so Tejero and Milans del Bosch acted in February 1981.
However, the coup failed when the king defended the Constitution, and the Cortes then cut the military budget.
Instability therefore had a paradoxical consequence: it ended in the defeat of the old right and a peaceful Socialist victory in 1982.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the roles of Suárez and Juan Carlos in Spain's transition to democracy between 1975 and 1981.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The roles of Suárez and Juan Carlos

modelPlan.thesis: Both were products of Franco's system who used the old regime's trust to dismantle it, but they played different roles: Suárez built democracy's institutions, while the king chose the builder and defended the result in 1981.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both reassured the old guard.
Difference: the king intervened at decisive moments.

modelPlan.counter: Suárez fell in January 1981 while the king's authority grew, suggesting the king's role mattered more in the long run.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? The king's stand in 1981, because without it Suárez's institutions might not have survived.

segments.text: Suárez and Juan Carlos were both Franco's men, but they played different parts in dismantling his regime.

Franco chose Juan Carlos as his successor and Suárez had headed the National Movement, yet Suárez legalised parties and unions in 1977, whereas the king appointed him in 1976 and rejected the coup in 1981.
This meant that Suárez built the institutions of democracy, while the king supplied the authority that protected them.
However, Suárez was forced out by his own party in January 1981, while the king's authority grew, so their roles were not equal over time.
The decisive difference was therefore the king's defence of the Constitution in 1981, which secured what Suárez had built.
